summary: Reliable and Available Wireless (RAW) extends DetNet reliability and availability to networks mixing wired and wireless segments. It builds on the DetNet architecture of RFC 8655 and adapts it to the challenges of wireless links.

plainLanguage.summary: Wireless links can be flaky. This explains how to build a network that still delivers messages on time using wired and wireless parts together.

subtitle: How to deliver packets reliably over networks that mix wired and wireless links.

tldr.problem: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) provides bounded latency and near-zero packet loss over wired networks, but wireless links are unreliable with intermittent losses and varying throughput, making DetNet guarantees difficult to maintain in mixed wired-wireless networks.
tldr.mechanism: RAW extends DetNet's architecture by introducing recovery graphs—topologies that contain multiple alternate paths within a defined region—and a Point of Local Repair (PLR) function that dynamically selects which path to use based on current link quality. RAW operates at a timescale between routing (slow) and forwarding (fast) to react to transient wireless degradation while avoiding oscillation from route churn.
tldr.outcome: Networks mixing wired and wireless segments can now meet deterministic service levels via path redundancy and dynamic selection, protecting against transient wireless losses without waiting for slow routing convergence or burning extra energy on constant retries.

today: RFC 9912 is Informational and was published in April 2026. It extends RFC 8655 (DetNet Architecture) to wireless networks and provides the conceptual foundation for RAW mechanisms. The RFC does not define specific protocols or messages; instead, it describes the architecture and principles that allow DetNet to work over mixed wired-wireless networks. Standards-track work to implement RAW (such as specific PLR algorithms or OAM protocols) is ongoing in the IETF and other standards bodies.

sections.title: The Wireless Challenge for Determinism
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet, RFC 8655) aims to deliver packets with bounded maximum latency and minimal packet loss, suitable for critical applications like factory automation and power grid control. DetNet was designed with wired networks in mind, where links are stable and packet delivery is predictable.

Wireless networks operate on a shared medium where interference, obstacles, and multipath fading cause intermittent transmission loss. A link might be good one moment and unusable the next, then recover seconds later. This transient behavior is fundamentally different from wired networks' consistency.

The RFC challenges DetNet to work over mixed wired-wireless networks without inventing new lower-layer wireless technologies. Instead, RAW extends DetNet's Network Plane with mechanisms to detect and react to wireless degradation quickly, using redundant paths and dynamic path selection. RAW assumes that lower layers (like Time-Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH) or OFDMA) can provide scheduled, deterministic transmission; RAW's job is to work around the gaps.
sections.plainLanguage: Wired networks are like a reliable highway; wireless is like a road with occasional rockslides. DetNet was built for the highway. RAW adds detour signs and makes traffic choose the best available route in real time.

sections.title: Recovery Graphs and Protection Paths
sections.content:
The RFC introduces two key concepts:

Recovery Graph: A topological region within which multiple alternate routes are available and pre-provisioned. Unlike a single IP path, a recovery graph contains multiple protection paths from an ingress to an egress node. The recovery graph is pre-computed and installed by the Controller Plane (the slow, offline routing system), but the actual forwarding path chosen within it changes dynamically based on link conditions.

A recovery graph contains DetNet relay nodes that perform PREOF (Packet Replication, Elimination, and Ordering Functions)—they can duplicate packets onto multiple paths and eliminate duplicates at the egress. Between relay nodes are segments of transit nodes that perform simple forwarding. The graph can be strict (every hop is controlled) or loose (RAW controls relay nodes, other hops may be opaque).

Protection Paths: Two or more end-to-end paths from ingress to egress within the recovery graph. In the simplest case (1+1 protection), there is a main path and a backup path. In more complex networks, a mesh topology offers many overlapping paths. The Point of Local Repair (PLR) function at the ingress (or at intermediate relay nodes) selects which protection path each packet should take, based on current link quality observations.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of computing one route and hoping it works, RAW pre-computes multiple routes and gives them all the resources they need. Then, for each packet, it decides on the fly which route looks best right now.

sections.title: The RAW Control Loop (OODA)
sections.content:
RAW operates a control loop following the OODA model (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act), running at a timescale between routing and forwarding:

Observe (RAW OAM): Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) collects link quality metrics—Packet Delivery Ratio (PDR), Link Quality Indicator (LQI), delay—for each hop in the recovery graph. OAM may be active (sending probe packets) or passive (monitoring user traffic).

Orient: The RAW-Extended DetNet Operational Plane analyzes the metrics and estimates which protection paths are currently viable given the observed link conditions. It assesses whether each path can meet the Service Level Objectives (SLOs) in terms of PDR and latency.

Decide: The Point of Local Repair (PLR) compares the protection paths and selects which one(s) to activate for the next set of packets. The decision may favor replication (send on multiple paths, pick the first to arrive) or single-path selection (choose the best path). The PLR avoids oscillation by dampening rapid changes—it does not reroute every packet, but rather makes decisions at a slower timescale than individual packet forwarding.

Act: The selected protection path(s) are activated via DetNet path selection mechanisms and reliability functions (PREOF). Packets are forwarded (and possibly duplicated and eliminated) according to the active paths.

This loop runs faster than routing convergence (which takes seconds or minutes) but slower than packet forwarding (which takes microseconds), allowing RAW to react to transient wireless failures without causing network oscillation.
sections.plainLanguage: Every few milliseconds, the network checks which routes are working. When a wireless link gets flaky, it automatically shifts traffic to a backup route, then back again when the link recovers. It does not obsess over every packet—it makes calm decisions at a middle-ground speed.

sections.title: Wireless Capabilities RAW Leverages
sections.content:
Unlike wired networks, wireless media have unique capabilities that RAW can exploit:

Promiscuous Overhearing: In wireless mesh or broadcast networks, multiple nodes can receive the same transmission. If node A sends to node B, node C might also hear it. RAW can leverage this by sending packets toward multiple potential next hops; the first one to arrive at the egress is accepted, and others are eliminated. This improves reliability without explicit retransmission.

L2-Aware Routing: Wireless link quality varies dynamically with interference, distance, and obstacles. RAW uses Link Quality Indicator (LQI) or similar metrics (RSSI, SNR, Expected Transmission Count (ETX)) from the lower layers to inform path selection. Routing based purely on hop count (shortest path) fails when links are flaky. RAW instead considers link quality metrics and may accept longer paths if they are more reliable.

Redundant Transmissions: Wireless networks commonly use Automatic Repeat Request (ARQ) at Layer 2 and Forward Error Correction (FEC) at the PHY layer. RAW can coexist with these by bounding the latency budget: a packet may be retransmitted twice at Layer 2, as long as the total latency remains within the SLO.

Relay Coordination and Constructive Interference: With fine time synchronization (as in TSCH), multiple relays can transmit the same packet and have the signal energy add up at the receiver, improving the received signal. RAW considers this opportunity when designing recovery graphs.
sections.plainLanguage: Wireless is not just a broken version of wired—it has special tricks. You can send the same message via multiple paths at once, you can hear neighbors' transmissions in the background, and you can coordinate transmissions to reinforce each other. RAW uses all of these.

sections.title: Service Level Objectives and Reliability Metrics
sections.content:
The RFC defines how RAW measures success:

Service Level Agreement (SLA): A contract specifying performance targets (e.g., "99.99% packet delivery" or "maximum 50 ms latency").

Service Level Objective (SLO): The target the network operator sets to meet the SLA (e.g., 99.999% internal PDR to account for edge losses).

Service Level Indicator (SLI): The measured metric (e.g., actual PDR observed on the network).

RAW must manage reliability (probability that a given packet is delivered) and availability (fraction of time the service meets its SLO). A service can be highly available (uptime is 99.99%) but not always deliver every packet; RAW's goal is to meet both metrics by dynamically choosing paths that avoid known failures and by replicating packets when a single path is too risky.

The RFC also distinguishes between maximum contiguous loss (how long the network can be broken before recovery) and PDR over long observation windows. Both matter for different applications: a power grid control system needs PDR, while a factory conveyor belt needs bounded loss duration.
sections.plainLanguage: RAW keeps a promise: "I will deliver this many packets, and I will do it within this much time." It measures constantly whether it is keeping the promise, and if not, it reroutes to a backup path.

sections.title: Applicability and Deployment
sections.content:
RAW is applicable to any network mixing wired and wireless, from factory automation with both wired switches and wireless sensors, to metropolitan mesh networks connecting buildings with wireless backhaul, to rural areas with satellite and wireless terrestrial links.

RAW does not mandate a specific wireless technology. It works with TSCH (Time-Slotted Channel Hopping), OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiple Access), Wi-Fi with QoS, cellular networks, or any technology that can provide deterministic scheduling at the lower layers.

The recovery graph is typically computed by the Controller Plane using a Path Computation Element (PCE) or YANG data model, informed by measurements of link quality. The PLR function can run at the ingress node for all flows in the recovery graph, or it can be distributed—each relay node making local decisions based on its observations. Distributed PLR is more scalable but requires careful design to avoid oscillations.

The RFC emphasizes that RAW is agnostic to the mechanism that establishes paths. Whether using RSVP, Segment Routing, or a centralized controller, RAW's contribution is the dynamic path selection and monitoring within the recovery graph.
sections.plainLanguage: RAW is a general principle that works with any wireless technology and any routing mechanism. It just says: pre-compute multiple routes, measure link quality in real time, and steer traffic to the best available route.

items.title: Promiscuous Overhearing
items.text: Multiple nodes hear the same transmission; first arrival eliminates need for retries.

items.title: L2-Aware Routing
items.text: Dynamic link quality metrics (LQI, ETX) guide path selection instead of static hop count.

items.title: Redundant Transmissions
items.text: Layer 2 ARQ and FEC coexist with RAW if bounded by latency budget.

items.title: Relay Coordination
items.text: Synchronized transmissions can constructively interfere to strengthen signal at receiver.
